what_its_for: Inotersen is used to treat nerve damage (called polyneuropathy) caused by a rare inherited disease called hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR amyloidosis). This disease causes an abnormal protein called transthyretin (TTR) to build up in your nerves and organs. Inotersen works by reducing the amount of this harmful protein your liver makes.
how_to_take: Inotersen is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), similar to how insulin is injected. You will be trained by your healthcare provider on how to inject it yourself at home. Inject it into your stomach (abdomen), thigh, or the back of your upper arm. Rotate injection sites each week — do not inject in the same spot twice in a row. Do not inject into skin that is bruised, red, tender, hard, or scarred. Allow the pre-filled syringe to come to room temperature for at least 30 minutes before injecting. Do not shake the syringe.
dosing: The usual dose is 284 mg injected under the skin once every week, on the same day each week. Your doctor will decide the best day for you. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Before starting and while taking this medicine, you must take a vitamin A supplement as directed by your doctor, because inotersen lowers vitamin A levels in your body.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been 3 days or fewer since your scheduled dose, take the missed dose as soon as you remember and then continue your normal weekly schedule. If it has been more than 3 days since your missed dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose on your regularly scheduled day. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store inotersen in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Do not use it if it has been frozen. Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 86°F or 30°C) for up to 6 weeks. Once removed from the refrigerator, do not put it back — use it within 6 weeks or throw it away. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children. Dispose of used syringes in a sharps container — ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid missing your regular blood and urine tests — these are required to monitor for serious side effects. Do not stop taking inotersen without talking to your doctor first. Avoid taking ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), aspirin, or other NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) without first checking with your doctor, as these can increase your risk of kidney problems and bleeding. Avoid activities that could cause injury, as this medicine can lower your platelet count and increase bleeding risk. Tell all your healthcare providers that you are taking inotersen before any procedure, surgery, or new medication.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of the following: unusual bruising or bleeding that does not stop (such as cuts, gums, or nosebleeds), blood in your urine (pink, red, or dark colored urine), blood in your stool (black or tarry stools), coughing or vomiting blood, sudden severe headache or confusion (could be signs of bleeding in the brain), signs of a serious allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing), signs of kidney problems (swelling in legs or ankles, decreased urination, foamy urine), or signs of low platelet count (tiny red or purple spots on skin, unexplained heavy bleeding). Also call your doctor if you develop any new or unusual symptoms.
when_it_works: Inotersen starts reducing the abnormal TTR protein in your body within a few weeks of starting treatment. However, improvements in nerve symptoms may take several months and vary from person to person. Some people experience stabilization of their condition rather than major improvement. It is important to keep taking your medication regularly, even if you do not feel different right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Inotersen may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if inotersen passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Older adults: Elderly patients may be more sensitive to side effects and will be monitored closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as dose adjustments or extra monitoring may be needed. Children: Inotersen is not approved for use in children.
